text: A chart is an answer to a question, so before you pick one, name the question. Most business questions fall into four families.

Comparing categories, like which segment spends the most, calls for a bar chart. Our eyes compare lengths from a shared baseline very accurately, so bars are the workhorse. A trend over time calls for a line chart: time runs left to right, and the joined points show direction and pace. A distribution, like how spend is spread across customers, calls for a histogram or a box plot. And a relationship between two numeric variables, do more orders mean more spend, calls for a scatter plot.

Here are three of them in a few lines of matplotlib, using our illustrative customer table of three hundred customers. A bar for average spend per segment, a histogram of spend, and a scatter of orders against spend.

Notice what each one shows. The bars say Premium customers spend the most. The histogram is right-skewed, with a long tail of big spenders. And the scatter shows a clear upward relationship: more orders, more spend. Same data, three questions, three charts.

A few traps to avoid. A pie chart with many slices is hard to read, so use a sorted bar chart instead, and save pies for two or three parts of a whole. Don't connect categories with a line, because a line implies order and continuity that isn't there. And when you're showing two numeric variables, use a scatter plot rather than paired bars. When in doubt, ask yourself: what should the reader compare?
